newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian chief vows fierce resistance to soft euro.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian chief vows fierce resistance to soft euro.

text.p: Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber vowed on Wednesday to put up "fierce resistance" to any attempt by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to soften the membership criteria for Europe's planned single currency.

In remarks in Wednesday's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper, Stoiber said his Christian Social Union (CSU), junior partners in Kohl's government, would not tolerate a budget deficit above 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"The party stands behind me," the paper quoted the regional state leader as saying.
The Maastricht Treaty which lays down the conditions for economic and monetary union (EMU) stipulates that members should not have a budget deficit of more than three percent of GDP.
While senior Kohl allies have hinted that this does not have to mean exactly 3.0 percent, the CSU has insisted anything else would weaken the new currency.

Stoiber's comments mark the latest interjection by the well-known eurosceptic, who has consistently played to voter fears of swapping the hard Deutschemark for an unknown European currency that could include countries such as Italy and Spain.

The CSU's stance prompted Kohl to approach a Bavarian representative at last week's EU summit in Amsterdam and accuse the party of "unusually foolish talk" about EMU, according to German newspaper reports.

Stoiber told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Kohl was no longer being clear on whether the entry criteria would be completely applied. The chancellor was leaving open the question of whether the criteria would determine the timetable, Stoiber said.

Stoiber said the new currency, the euro, must be as strong as possible so citizens were not deprived of the value of their life savings. If the CSU did not insist on stability, it would be committing "the biggest breach of confidence in its history".
He said the figure of 3.0 percent was a "synonym for the culture of stability".

Bonn would have to come into conflict with Paris if the new French government made use of the "classic French philosophy" that even monetary instability could be counted as a political instrument, Stoiber said.
